Figure 1a from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

In *Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist* [[1]](#ref-1) (*Nature*, May 2026), [Juraj Gottweis](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2051681709), [Wei-Hung Weng](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2239098855), [Alexander Daryin](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2347345594), [Tao Tu](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2367117462), and five other co-first authors, with senior authors including [Vivek Natarajan](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/144223091), [Demis Hassabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demis_Hassabis), [James Manyika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Manyika), [Yossi Matias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yossi_Matias), and [Pushmeet Kohli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pushmeet_Kohli), and roughly 50 co-authors across Google DeepMind, Google Research, Google Cloud AI Research, Stanford University School of Medicine, Houston Methodist, and Imperial College London, introduce Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based system that proposes research hypotheses and ranks them in a tournament that improves the survivors.

> Scientific discovery is driven by scientists generating novel hypotheses for complex problems that undergo rigorous experimental validation. To augment this process, we introduce *Co-Scientist, a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini for structured scientific thinking and hypothesis generation*. Co-Scientist aims to help scientists discover new original knowledge. Conditioned on their research objectives and prior scientific evidence, it formulates demonstrably novel research hypotheses for experimental verification. The system's design involves agents continuously generating, critiquing and refining hypotheses accelerated by scaling test-time compute. Key contributions include: *(1) a multi-agent architecture with an asynchronous task execution framework for flexible compute scaling; (2) a tournament evolution process for self-improving hypotheses generation*. Automated evaluations show continued benefits of test-time compute scaling, improving hypothesis quality over time. While general purpose, we focus the validation in three biomedical applications: *drug repurposing, novel target discovery, and explaining mechanisms of anti-microbial resistance*. Specifically, Co-Scientist helped identify new drug repurposing candidates and synergistic combination therapies for *acute myeloid leukemia, which were validated through in vitro experiments*. These real-world validations demonstrate the potential of Co-Scientist to accelerate scientific discovery and usher in an era of AI empowered scientists.

## Method

Co-Scientist is a compound, multi-agent system built on Gemini, run as a "scientist in the loop": a researcher states a goal in natural language, sets constraints, and can steer the search or seed hypotheses as it works. The system generates and ranks hypotheses, but the experimental validation stays with people: every proposal passes human expert review and wet-lab assays before it is confirmed.

- **Six specialized agents under a supervisor.** A Supervisor agent parses the goal and assigns six worker agents (Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, and Meta-review) to an asynchronous task queue, all sharing a persistent context memory. The agents are not separate models: they all run on the same base LLM (Gemini 2.0 here) and differ only by their prompts, and the framework is model-agnostic. Every hypothesis must meet default criteria: plausibility, novelty, testability, and safety.
- **Grounding and critique.** The Generation agent drafts hypotheses from literature search and simulated scientific debate. The Reflection agent then reviews them as a peer reviewer would, and its access to web search and specialized AI models is what kept hallucinated, implausible hypotheses down.
- **Fitness is winning debates.** Hypotheses are scored by an internal [Elo rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elo_rating_system) — the chess-style score that ranks competitors, here hypotheses, by who wins pairwise matchups. The Ranking agent stages those matchups as multi-turn scientific debates (single-turn for lower-ranked pairs), judged on correctness, novelty, and testability. A new hypothesis enters at an Elo of 1200 and climbs or falls by its record. The Proximity agent clusters similar hypotheses so the debates pit close rivals against each other.
- **Evolution reproduces rather than overwrites.** The Evolution agent builds *new* hypotheses from the top-ranked ones: combining the strongest parts of several (the crossover analog), spinning off variants inspired by one or more parents, regrounding them in fresh literature, simplifying them, or forcing deliberately divergent "out-of-the-box" ideas (the mutation analog). It never edits a hypothesis in place, so strong parents survive and every offspring has to earn its own Elo back in the tournament.
- **It improves without retraining.** A Meta-review agent distills recurring weaknesses from the reviews and debates and appends that feedback to every agent's prompt on the next round, so the system learns by updating its context rather than its weights, with no fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. An asynchronous framework lets it spend more test-time compute on a goal, with the Supervisor tracking progress through periodic summary statistics and deciding when a run hits a terminal state. There is no convergence threshold: quality (Elo) never saturated in the paper's runs, so they ended on a compute budget rather than because the system stopped improving.

## Results

The paper validates Co-Scientist with automated benchmarks and end-to-end wet-lab experiments in three biomedical areas, all run with experts in the loop. [[1]](#ref-1)

- **Quality climbs with test-time compute.** Across 203 research goals, both the average and best Elo ratings rose the longer the system reasoned, with no sign of saturation.
- **Beats frontier reasoning models.** On 15 expert-curated goals, Co-Scientist's Elo eventually surpassed Gemini 2.0 Pro and Flash Thinking, OpenAI o1 and o3-mini-high, and DeepSeek R1.
- **Experts preferred its output.** On 11 goals, Co-Scientist scored an average preference rank of 2.36 and novelty and impact ratings of 3.64 and 3.09 out of 5, and was the top pick of all four LLM judges.

![Hypothesis quality rises with test-time compute: best and top-10 average Elo climb across reasoning time (a); on 15 expert-curated goals Co-Scientist's Elo eventually passes the frontier reasoning models (b); and domain experts rated its hypotheses highest on novelty, impact, and overall preference (c). Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure2.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure2-full.jpg"}

- **AML drug repurposing.** Co-Scientist generated repurposing hypotheses across a curated list of 2,300 approved drugs spanning 34 cancer types. After expert oncologists reviewed and ranked its predictions, five candidates were tested in vitro, and three (binimetinib, pacritinib, cerivastatin) inhibited acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cell viability. Binimetinib, approved for metastatic melanoma, reached a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50, the dose that cuts cell survival in half, so lower means more potent) as low as 2 nM in all AML lines but NOMO-1, while leaving a non-leukemia control line largely unharmed.
- **Novel single-agent candidates.** With no prior preclinical evidence or human feedback, Co-Scientist proposed three wholly new picks: nanvuranlat, KIRA6, and leflunomide. KIRA6, which blocks a cellular stress sensor (the enzyme IRE1α), had an 18-fold safety margin: it killed the stem-cell-like KG-1a leukemia cells at one-eighteenth the dose that affected healthy control cells (an IC50 of 10 nM against 180 nM).

![Dose-response curves for the AML repurposing candidates: binimetinib, pacritinib, and cerivastatin against MOLM-13 (a-c), and the wholly novel pick KIRA6 across four AML subtypes and the non-AML TK6 control (d-h). Figure 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure3.jpg){fig-align="center"}

- **Synergistic combinations.** Co-Scientist also proposed multi-drug regimens, and of seven it suggested, the two- and three-drug combinations were mostly synergistic in one leukemia line (MOLM-13), meaning the drugs together killed more cells than the sum of each alone, while the harder-to-treat KG-1a line responded inconsistently.

![Synergy analysis of Co-Scientist's proposed combinations: the JNJ-64619178 + selinexor dual combination falls well inside the synergy zone in MOLM-13 and KG-1a (a, b), and excess-effect heatmaps for the JQ1 + olaparib + MSA2 triple show synergy in MOLM-13 but antagonism in KG-1a (c, d). Figure 4 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure4.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure4-full.jpg"}

- **Liver fibrosis and antimicrobial resistance.** In lab-grown mini-livers (hepatic organoids), Co-Scientist proposed three epigenetic targets (genes that switch other genes on or off), and drugs against two of them reduced scarring without harming the tissue (one, vorinostat, is already an approved cancer drug). For antimicrobial resistance, it worked out in about two days how a family of mobile DNA elements that ferry resistance genes between bacteria (cf-PICIs) jump across species, by borrowing the tail proteins of different viruses, matching an unpublished experiment that was running at the same time.

## My Notes

- **Both Nature papers point to the same lesson: grounding beats the raw model.** Co-Scientist's own ablation found that giving the Reflection agent access to external search tools is what prevented hallucinated, implausible hypotheses [[1]](#ref-1) — the gains came from disciplined literature retrieval rather than a bigger base model. [FutureHouse's Robin](/posts/20260606-robin-multi-agent-scientific-discovery/) [[2]](#ref-2), in *Nature* the same week, reached the comparable conclusion automating discovery for macular degeneration. Two independently built systems converging on the same point is the part worth remembering.

- **The Elo curve is self-evaluated.** It is scored by the same model that generates the hypotheses, so a rising Elo means later hypotheses beat earlier ones in the model's own debates — an internal-consistency signal that can optimize for what the judge likes rather than what is true. The only anchor to real quality is the small human-expert correlation on 11 goals. The wet-lab hits are the harder evidence.
